title: Developing, Analyzing, and Using Distractors for Multiple-Choice Tests in Education: A Comprehensive Review https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2017-50122-003
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 10, 2025 — original paper:
summary: This paper, reviewed by Barton, is a Review of Educational Research literature synthesis on how to create, analyze, and use distractors — the incorrect options — in multiple-choice tests. It covers strategies for developing distractors from common misconceptions, psychometric methods (classical test theory and item response theory) for evaluating whether distractors are doing their job, and recommendations on the optimal number and placement of distractors. The review concludes that two distractors plus one correct answer is often the optimal format, reducing both test-development time and student test-taking time without sacrificing item quality. It also covers automatic item generation and 'key features' methods as emerging techniques for producing large volumes of well-constructed distractors at scale.
points: Distractors should be built from real student misconceptions — gathered from open-ended responses, verbal reports, or known error patterns — rather than invented arbitrarily.
A distractor chosen by fewer than 5% of students is likely nonfunctioning and needs revision; the point-biserial correlation and choice-mean comparisons are two additional diagnostic tools.
Two distractors plus one correct answer is frequently the optimal number of options, cutting development and testing time while preserving item quality.
Analyzing which distractor students pick gives teachers diagnostic information about specific misunderstandings, turning the wrong-answer data into an instructional signal.
quotes: This literature review from the Review of Educational Research examines the creation, analysis, and use of distractors in multiple-choice tests.

Teachers should focus on creating plausible distractors that reflect common student misconceptions or errors in thinking. This can be achieved by reviewing students' responses to open-ended questions, using verbal reports, or considering typical student errors.
Distractors chosen by less than 5% of students might be nonfunctioning and need revision.
Teachers can use the point-biserial correlation to evaluate the effectiveness of distractors. A value greater than -0.05 indicates a distractor is not discriminating adequately.
There is evidence that using two distractors and one correct option is often optimal. This can reduce test development time, reduce student test-taking time, and improve item quality.
Multiple-choice testing is considered one of the most effective and enduring forms of educational assessment that remains in practice today
